title: Complex chronic care management billed for 257 patients in October 2026
what_we_see: In October 2026 the practice billed the complex care-management code (99487) for 257 patients, 213 of them with the add-on code (99489), all under the physician. That is 79% of the 326 patients with any charge that month. The claims assert 21,810 minutes, about 364 hours, of care-management time in one month. That is the full working month of about two people. The practice's whole staff payroll, including the nurse practitioner, was about $17,000 a month in the first nine months of 2026. A reviewer would ask who logged the hours, whether they were employees or contractors, and where the time is recorded. Nationally the complex code is about 8% of care-management claims. At this pace the practice would bill about 0.5% of all complex care management Medicare paid in the country in 2024. Its 152 claims a month in a skilled-facility setting would equal about 6% of the 2024 national total paid at the facility rate. Service dates are batched at month end. Only 42% of lines have been paid since June. In Medicare's public data the practice billed 1,300 to 2,050 of these a year from 2019 to 2022, 539 in 2023 and none in 2024. Care management has some of the highest error rates Medicare measures: in the 2025 review 65% of payments for the standard code (99490) and 75% for the physician-time code (99491) were improper, almost all for missing or insufficient documentation. No rate is published for the complex code. The Florida Medicare contractor lists care management (99490 and 99491) as an active targeted review. On April 30, 2026 a Florida physician and practice agreed to a five-year exclusion from federal health programs after the Inspector General alleged they billed care management, including both complex codes, that was not rendered.
rule: Each claim requires: two or more chronic conditions expected to last at least 12 months that put the patient at significant risk of death, decline or flare-up; a visit at which care management was discussed, if the patient is new or was not seen in the past year; the patient's consent, recorded before care management starts; a comprehensive care plan, with a copy given or made available to the patient or caregiver; at least 60 minutes that month of care-management time by clinical staff under the billing practitioner's direction (30 more for each add-on), toward which the practitioner's own time also counts; and medical decisions of moderate or high complexity by that practitioner. Staff must be the practice's own or under contract to it. Time by a facility's nurses does not count. Only one practitioner may bill per patient per month. The service may be billed for residents of nursing and assisted living facilities. Whether it may be billed for a month a resident spends in a Medicare Part A skilled stay is not settled. A 2016 Medicare question-and-answer sheet said no, and the current one does not repeat that limit.
exposure: Going forward, the whole revenue line: about $165,000 a year at October's volume and today's paid rate, and about $370,000 a year if every line were paid. Looking back, public data show about $490,000 of complex care management allowed by Medicare under the physician for 2021 through 2023, all inside the six-year lookback today. Medicare pays about 80% of an allowed amount. Any of it that records do not support would have to be repaid. A pattern of claims that do not meet Medicare's rules can also cost a practice its Medicare billing privileges. Volume this far from the norm is what Medicare's program-integrity contractors screen for. A buyer would exclude this revenue unless it is documented.
recommended_review: Hold the next monthly batch now and engage the attorney. Have the attorney direct a first look at 30 patient-months chosen at random by someone other than the billing physician. For each, find the consent and its date, the starting visit if one was required, the care plan, a time log showing who did what on which day and for how long, and the physician's decision making. Add up one month of logged minutes and compare them with the hours the staff and the physician actually had. Agree with the attorney, before the look begins, what result will trigger a review of past claims. Release a held claim only when that patient's own records support it.
control: Bill care management only from a time log, at the code the logged minutes support (standard care management needs 20 minutes). Each month compare total minutes billed with staff hours available. Record consent as a required field. Set the place of service from the resident's status. Never use a date of service after the patient's date of death. For a month in which a patient died, left the practice's care or elected hospice, bill only if the full time was logged before that day. Do not bill care management in a month when hospice or home health supervision (G0182 or G0181) is billed.

title: Visit levels far above national patterns in the hospital and nursing facilities
what_we_see: Subsequent hospital visits were billed at the top level (99233) 73.7% of the time, against 37.2% nationally. Every initial hospital visit was the top level (99223), against 59.5%. Subsequent nursing facility visits were the second-highest level (99309) 95.6% of the time, against 48.8%, and every initial nursing facility visit was the top level (99306), against 48.5%. Both discharge-day families were billed only at the longer code. All 31 assisted living visits were billed with a new-patient code (99344), 25 of them by the nurse practitioner, and none with an established-patient code, although 103 assisted living residents were billed care management in October. In CMS data the physician's top-level share of hospital follow-up visits was 64.5% in 2023, 1.3% in 2024 and is 73.7% now. As billed, the physician's work units run near three times the family medicine median. In October there were 218 visits to 135 nursing facility residents, 1.6 each. Fourteen residents were seen four or more times. Each visit needs a medical reason in the note. Visits with no documented reason for their frequency were the most common failure in the Inspector General's 2026 audit, which sampled residents seen three or more times in a month.
rule: The level of a visit must follow the complexity of medical decision making, or total time, that the note documents for that day, and the service must be medically necessary. A sick population can justify a high average. It does not justify the same level on nearly every visit.
exposure: The difference between adjacent levels is roughly $20 to $45 a visit. On about 6,000 visits a year, a finding that half were one level high would be on the order of $60,000 to $100,000 a year, and Medicare contractors extrapolate from samples. Nationally, 25.5% of the dollars paid for the top initial nursing facility code, which this practice bills on every admission, were improper in Medicare's 2025 review. In Medicare's 2025 review, 22.7% of payments for the top subsequent hospital code (99233), the practice's most-billed visit code, were improper. The Florida Medicare contractor lists hospital visits (99221 to 99223 and 99231 to 99233) as an active targeted review. In July 2026 the Inspector General reported on 60 sampled patient-months of nursing home visits, each with 3 to 10 visits, paid by another contractor in 2018 and 2019. Forty-two failed review: 24 because the visits were not medically necessary, 13 for coding and 10 for missing or insufficient records. A nationwide audit of these services opened in April 2026.
recommended_review: Through the attorney, hire an independent certified auditor to review 10 notes per code family for each clinician, about 80 to 100 notes, chosen at random from the last six months. Ask for under-coding as well as over-coding. Include 10 assisted living visits and check each patient's history for an earlier visit by the practice. Agree with the attorney beforehand what error rate will trigger a larger, statistically valid sample. The Inspector General's self-disclosure protocol asks for at least 100 claims.
control: Quarterly audit of 10 charts per clinician. A monthly table of each clinician's level mix against the national mix. Coding education built from the audit's findings. Levels chosen by the clinician in the note, never changed downstream.

title: Every nursing facility visit billed as a Medicare Part A skilled stay
what_we_see: All nursing facility visits and 152 of October's care-management lines carry place of service 31, the code for a patient in a Medicare Part A covered skilled stay. Place of service 32, for residents who are not in such a stay, was never used. With five facilities and many long-term residents, a large share of these claims almost certainly name the wrong setting.
rule: Medicare's manual says to use place of service 31 when the patient is in a Part A skilled stay and 32 when the patient is not, even in the same building. The setting changes the payment rate: 31 pays the facility rate and 32 the non-facility rate.
exposure: In 2026 Medicare paid nursing facility visit codes 12% to 15% less under code 31 than under code 32, so each visit to a long-term resident billed as a skilled stay was underpaid. On about 2,600 nursing facility visits a year that is roughly $10,000 to $25,000 for 2026, depending on how many residents were long-term. A paid claim is corrected by asking the Medicare contractor to reopen it. First Coast accepts that request for any reason within one year of the original payment decision. After that it needs good cause, up to four years. For 2027 Medicare set the two rates equal for visits. For complex care management the facility rate was about 44% lower in 2026 ($81 against $143 for code 99487 in this area). Wrong setting codes also undermine the practice's credibility in any audit.
recommended_review: Ask each facility for a current census showing which residents are in a Part A skilled stay. Compare with the last three months of claims and count how many carried the wrong code and the payment difference in each direction.
control: A weekly census from every facility with skilled-stay status and payer, stored with the patient, from which the billing routine sets place of service for each date of service.

title: Initial nursing facility visits billed by the nurse practitioner in skilled stays
what_we_see: The nurse practitioner billed 10 of the 19 initial nursing facility visits in the charge feed, all at the top level and all as skilled stays. CMS data show she billed that code 37 times in 2023 and 129 times in 2024. In the 2024 public data, which leaves out rows with fewer than 11 patients, the physician billed 102 nursing facility visits of any kind. That is fewer than the 129 initial visits the nurse practitioner billed. That gap is the first thing to explain.
rule: A nurse practitioner may bill an initial nursing facility code for a medically necessary first evaluation. But in a skilled nursing facility the physician must personally perform the federally required initial comprehensive visit, no later than 30 days after admission, and may not delegate it. After that visit, alternate required visits may be delegated. For residents who are not in a Part A stay, federal rules leave this to the State. Florida's nursing home rule allows required visits by a physician or another licensed health professional, but it lets the physician hand over his part of the care only after the required visit. Ask the attorney how that applies to the first visit.
exposure: If the nurse practitioner's visit was the only comprehensive visit in a Medicare Part A skilled stay, the facility is out of compliance with its survey rule and the physician has not made a visit he must make in person. The nurse practitioner's own claim can still be valid as a medically necessary visit. Facilities are cited for this, and it can cost a medical directorship or the relationship.
recommended_review: For each skilled admission in the last six months where the nurse practitioner did the first visit, find the date and note of the physician's own comprehensive visit.
control: Track, for every skilled admission, the due date and the completion date of the physician's comprehensive visit, and the 30-day and 60-day visits that follow.

title: No coding audit and no compliance program on record
what_we_see: The practice has written billing rules and runs the monthly exclusion check. Nothing else of a compliance program is evidenced: no named compliance contact, no training record, no audit, no log of problems found and fixed. Billing is run by software agents under standing rules that include automatic write-offs and re-dating denied care-management claims.
rule: A compliance program is voluntary for a small practice, but federal guidance describes seven elements and treats a working program as evidence of good faith. The duty to return overpayments is not voluntary. Since 2025 it is triggered when a practice knows of an overpayment, deliberately avoids learning of one, or recklessly disregards the signs.
exposure: Without a program the practice cannot show that an error was an honest mistake caught by its own controls. That record is one of the things that can make the difference between a refund and penalties.
recommended_review: With the attorney, write a short program sized to two clinicians. Start with the audit, because its results decide everything else.
control: A named compliance contact who, where possible, is not the owner and does not prepare claims (a staff member or an outside consultant), reporting to the owner each quarter. An annual training hour, a quarterly chart audit, a log of issues and corrections, and a yearly review of the billing rulebook by the auditor.

title: Possible overpayments with a legal deadline once identified
what_we_see: Three patterns in this review could each mean Medicare paid more than the records support: complex care management, visit levels and advance care planning. Two others raise different questions. If long-term residents were billed as skilled stays, Medicare paid less in 2026, not more. The nurse practitioner's initial visits raise a facility rule, not a payment rule. None has been tested against charts.
rule: A provider must report and return an overpayment within 60 days of identifying it. Since January 1, 2025 an overpayment is identified when the provider knows of it, deliberately avoids learning of it, or recklessly disregards the information in hand. That is the False Claims Act meaning of "knowingly". Once a first overpayment is identified, a timely, good-faith investigation of related overpayments suspends the deadline until the total is calculated or 180 days after that first identification, whichever comes first. The lookback is six years.
exposure: Money kept after the deadline can become a false claim: three times the amount plus a penalty of $14,308 to $28,619 for each claim at current levels. Acting promptly and on advice keeps a billing problem a refund.
recommended_review: Have the attorney open and direct the review, and set the sample plan with the auditor. Give the attorney the history first: why complex care management stopped after 2023, why top-level hospital visits fell to 1.3% in 2024, and any audit, record request, denial pattern or advice from that time. Earlier notice changes the legal position. Record the date the review starts and the date each overpayment is identified. The 60 days run from identification. A prompt, good-faith review of related claims pauses them from the day it starts, for no more than 180 days after the first identification.
control: A standing rule: any audit finding of an overpayment goes to the attorney the same week, with a dated record of what was decided. The attorney chooses the route: a voluntary refund to the Medicare contractor for an ordinary error, the Inspector General's self-disclosure protocol where penalties could apply (at least 1.5 times what Medicare paid, and never less than $20,000), or the Medicare agency's protocol for a problem under the self-referral law alone. The deadline to return the money is suspended once a protocol filing is acknowledged or an extended repayment schedule is requested.

title: Medical director payments from facilities where the practice also treats residents
what_we_see: The practice received two medical director stipends in the first nine months of 2026, $12,000 each. The data in hand do not name the payers. If they are facilities whose residents the practice also treats and bills for, the payments must fit the rule below. Whether written agreements, fair-market-value support and time records exist has not been confirmed.
rule: A physician who is paid by a facility and also sends it business (admissions, therapy orders, certifications of skilled care) has a financial relationship that must fit an exception to the federal self-referral law and should fit an Anti-Kickback safe harbor: a signed written agreement of at least a year, pay set in advance at fair market value, not tied to the volume or value of referrals, and for services actually performed and documented. Florida's kickback and patient-brokering laws cover referrals in either direction, for every payer.
exposure: If an agreement fails the exception, the facility may not bill Medicare for the designated services the physician ordered there, such as therapy billed to Part B, and must repay what it collected. The physician can face a civil penalty for each such service he knew or should have known was barred. Under the Anti-Kickback Statute, a claim that results from a kickback counts as a false claim, and penalties and exclusion can follow. Regulators have specifically warned about medical director agreements with little documented work.
recommended_review: Collect every medical director agreement from the past six years, not only the two current ones, with the fair-market-value support and time records for each. Stipends were $185,300 in 2023. Have the attorney confirm each fits the personal services exception and safe harbor. If a directorship is at a nursing home, check it against Florida's rule: medical director certification held or in progress, a documented facility visit every month, and a quarterly meeting with the facility's risk and quality committee.
control: A monthly time log for each directorship, signed by the physician and sent to the facility, and a calendar reminder 90 days before each agreement ends.

title: Enrollment and credentialing gaps, with a Medicaid deadline on December 1
what_we_see: At least nine enrollment problems are open. The physician's Florida Medicaid provider agreement renewal is due December 1, 2026 and the nurse practitioner's revalidation was returned incomplete. A commercial plan terminated the practice after a missed recredentialing. Railroad Medicare claims are being written off because the practice is not enrolled. The nurse practitioner's national provider record is out of date.
rule: A claim is payable only if the clinician was enrolled with that payer on the date of service. Florida Medicaid enrollment is what lets the practice be paid by Medicaid and by Medicaid managed care plans, and order or refer services for Medicaid patients. It adds little secondary payment on dual-eligible patients, who are about four in ten of the practice's Medicare patients: Florida pays nothing toward Medicare coinsurance when Medicare has already paid at least the Medicaid rate.
exposure: Denied Medicaid and Medicaid-plan claims until fixed, a plan's duty to drop a provider who is not enrolled with the State, denied claims for services the physician orders for Medicaid patients, and services that can never be billed for the gap period. 108 denied visits are already tagged credentialing.
recommended_review: File the Medicaid renewal this week and confirm receipt. Then rank the remaining items by dollars affected.
control: One calendar of every enrollment, license and registration expiry for both clinicians with 90-day warnings, checked at the monthly review.

title: The practice depends on one physician and a few sites
what_we_see: The owner bills 76.8% of charges, holds the facility and hospital relationships, manages the finances and maintains the billing rulebook. One hospital is 37.8% of charges and the top three sites are 64.8%. Medical director stipends have fallen from $185,300 in 2023 to about $32,000 a year.
rule: This is a business risk, not a rule. Insurers, lenders and buyers all ask the same question: what happens to revenue if the owner is out, or if the largest site changes its physician coverage.
exposure: An illness, a change of hospital administration or the loss of one facility could remove a third or more of revenue within weeks. The same dependence is the main reason a buyer would discount the price.
recommended_review: Write down what would happen in each case and what it would cost.
control: A covering physician under written agreement, a second clinician known at every site, disability and key-person insurance, and written agreements with the main facilities.

title: Software agents act on billing rules that have not been independently reviewed
what_we_see: Agents enter charges, send claims, post payments, re-send denied claims and write off old balances every few hours under a written rulebook. Rules include writing off balances over a year old ($40,686 on November 2, 2026) and re-dating a care-management claim to month end after a frequency denial. This application also allows anyone to create a sign-in, although only approved addresses can see data.
rule: The practice is responsible for every claim submitted in its name, whoever or whatever prepares it. Under the False Claims Act, knowing includes reckless disregard, with no proof of intent needed. Florida's Medicaid law gives the provider an affirmative duty to supervise the preparation and submission of claims. Changing a code, date, modifier or diagnosis after a denial is acceptable only when the record supports the change and a qualified person has checked it. A Medicare denial is a payment decision. It stands unless it is reopened or appealed. A claim is sent again only when it was rejected as incomplete or when First Coast's instructions for that denial say to resubmit. Re-sending paid or denied claims produces duplicate denials, and the share of claims denied is one of the things Medicare weighs when it decides whether to revoke billing privileges. Routinely waiving Medicare copayments and deductibles is unlawful. A patient's balance may be written off for documented hardship or after a real effort to collect has failed. The opposite rule applies to Qualified Medicare Beneficiaries, a group that includes most dual-eligible patients nationally: federal law forbids billing them for Medicare cost sharing at all. Every write-off therefore needs a reason code.
exposure: An automated rule that is wrong is wrong on every claim it touches, and it leaves a complete log of having done so. In 2025 a physician group paid $45 million over allegations that its billing software was set to bill the higher-paid service every time.
recommended_review: Have the coding auditor read every rule that changes a code, date, modifier, diagnosis, place of service or balance. Sample 25 automated actions against the charts. Confirm that the automatic write-off rule touches insurance balances only and records a reason. List every rule that re-sends a claim Medicare has already paid or denied. Check each against First Coast's instructions: reopening, appeal or, where allowed, a corrected new claim.
control: The owner's written approval for any rule that changes a claim's code, date, modifier, diagnosis, place of service or balance. A monthly sample of automated actions. Open sign-up turned off and access keys rotated.

title: Unknown status in Medicare's quality payment program
what_we_see: Neither clinician's status in the Merit-based Incentive Payment System is known. In 2024 each clinician exceeded all three low-volume limits ($90,000 of allowed charges, 200 patients, 200 services), and Medicare paid the two about $350,000.
rule: Eligible clinicians who do not report receive the maximum negative adjustment, 9% of Medicare Part B payments, two years after the performance year. In a small practice the electronic-records category is dropped automatically and quality can be reported on claims. A clinician who does 75% or more of his Medicare services in a hospital is scored on the hospital's results for quality and cost with nothing to submit. That may apply to the physician, but it may not be enough by itself to avoid a penalty. No exception covers a practice that simply did not report. The exception application is for rare events outside the practice's control, and for 2026 it closes December 31, 2026.
recommended_review: Look up both clinicians in the participation status tool, read the latest performance feedback, and note the reporting deadline for the 2026 performance year.
control: Each January, confirm status for the year just starting and choose the measures. Collect quality data all year. Start an improvement activity early enough to run 90 days in a row before December 31. Submit by March 31 of the following year.

title: Thin cash and expensive debt against an audit or a lost site
what_we_see: Cash covers about 48 days of spending. The main loan costs 13.99%. The owner drew $311,241 in salary and distributions in nine months and owes the corporation $162,121.
rule: Not a rule. Medicare can suspend payments or require repayment during an audit, and it is 55.5% of charges.
exposure: A payment hold or a refund demand of even $100,000 would exceed the cash on hand.
recommended_review: With the accountant, set a cash floor and a plan for the loan and the amount owed by the owner.
control: A 13-week cash forecast, a 90-day cash floor before distributions, and an unused line of credit.

title: Advance care planning billed without a tested record of time and consent
what_we_see: Advance care planning (99497) was billed on 62 encounters in the charge feed, about 8% of face-to-face visits, usually on the same day as an admission or another visit. In CMS data the two clinicians billed it about 650 to 880 times a year from 2019 to 2024. In the 2024 public data the nurse practitioner billed it 610 times against about 1,950 visits, including 168 times against 210 home or assisted living visits, and the two clinicians billed 878 claims for at most 614 patients. Whether each note records the time and who took part has not been checked.
rule: The conversation must be voluntary, and the note should say so, explain advance directives, name who was present, and state the minutes. The first code needs at least 16 minutes. Billing it again for the same patient needs a documented change in health or wishes. Time counted here cannot also count toward the visit billed the same day. From January 1, 2027, planning done by staff uses separate codes.
exposure: Nationally 29.8% of the dollars paid for this code were improper in Medicare's 2025 review, nine in ten for insufficient documentation. A claim with no time recorded can be denied in full. At 650 to 880 claims a year, Medicare allowed about $55,000 a year for these, and about $220,000 in the public data for 2021 through 2024. It is an easy finding for a reviewer.
recommended_review: Include 10 advance care planning notes in the outside audit.
control: A note template that will not release the code without minutes, participants and a statement that the discussion was voluntary.
